claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Controlled slow thermal treatment causes diffusion-controlled elemental partitioning in the alloy.
Diffusion-controlled partitioning creates localized compositional fluctuations.
Localized compositional fluctuations lower the nucleation barrier for secondary phases.
Partitioning occurs within grain interiors and at grain boundaries.
Al and Co diffuse faster than the other relevant constituents under the proposed treatment.
During slow cooling with intermediate holds, Al and Co segregate into localized regions of altered composition.
The segregated regions have a reduced free-energy barrier for secondary-phase nucleation.
Ordered FCC or B2 secondary phases can emerge from the partitioned regions.
Ordered FCC or B2 secondary phases are absent in the rapidly quenched baseline.
Slow cooling at 1–10 °C/min with dwell times between 1100 °C and 700 °C facilitates elemental diffusion relative to rapid quenching.
Slow-cooled and held samples will have a higher secondary-phase volume fraction than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled and held samples will exhibit a distinct secondary-phase morphology relative to rapidly quenched samples.
Localized elemental segregation will be detectable after slow cooling with intermediate holds.
Rapid quenching kinetically preserves the high-temperature BCC phase without significant elemental partitioning.
The proposed partitioning mechanism operates in a diffusion-active window between approximately 1100 °C and 700 °C.
The proposed mechanism should not operate when cooling is too rapid for appreciable diffusion.
The proposed mechanism should not operate at temperatures where diffusion is negligibly slow.
